highlights.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # ResCity-LLM Pipeline Turns Urban Resilience Knowledge Into Specialized AI Models ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=80&r=g) ![ResCity-LLM Pipeline Turns Urban Resilience Knowledge Into Specialized AI Models](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/stackrss-featured-14422-750x422.png) ResCity-LLM Pipeline Turns Urban Resilience Knowledge Into Specialized AI Models A team of urban resilience and earthquake engineering researchers has unveiled a complete pipeline for building large language models that can absorb the sprawling, fragmented knowledge of resilient cities and then deploy it across professional disaster-prevention tasks. The framework, called ResCity-LLM, links together four stages that had previously existed in isolation: assembling a domain corpus, generating training data automatically, adapting open-source models through a two-stage training strategy, and evaluating the results on a purpose-built benchmark. When the strongest adapted model was tested against two much larger general-purpose systems, it came out ahead on the benchmark’s overall weighted score, offering early evidence that compact, locally deployable models can compete with cloud giants in a specialized engineering domain. The motivation stems from an uncomfortable mismatch between what urban resilience research demands and what general-purpose language models are trained to do. Urban resilience draws on engineering, environment, planning, ecology, economics, sociology and governance simultaneously, with relevant knowledge scattered across academic papers, technical standards, planning documents, policy texts and case studies. General-purpose models such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek and Claude are trained overwhelmingly on general text, so they struggle to cover the complex knowledge structures, specialized semantics and typical task scenarios of this interdisciplinary field. Unlike medicine or law, where domain-specific language model research is relatively mature, resilience-oriented work had remained scattered and exploratory, lacking a systematic framework that spans corpus organization, training data construction, model training and specialized benchmark evaluation. The first ingredient is a data foundation the researchers call ResCity-Corpus. Using keywords related to urban and resilient cities in both English and Chinese, the team harvested academic literature from Elsevier, Nature, Springer, arXiv and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure, crawled news reports from mainstream media platforms, and collected professional monographs together with national, industry and local technical standards covering disaster prevention, urban lifeline systems and related fields. The final processed corpus for continued pre-training contained 60,059 text blocks amounting to 96.80 million tokens, split roughly 69 percent English and 31 percent Chinese, and organized into seven thematic categories ranging from hazard and climate science to governance and public policy. Raw corpora of this kind are notoriously messy, so the researchers designed what they call a multi-agent collaborative dual-stage data generation pipeline. In the first stage, aimed at continued pre-training, a clean-agent parses heterogeneous documents and strips out noise, a chunk-agent segments long texts into semantically coherent units sized by tokenizer length with overlapping tails to preserve context, a quality-agent powered by a commercial language model scores each chunk and flags low-quality or incomplete samples, and a repair-agent performs minimal fixes to broken sentences and grammatical errors without altering the underlying knowledge content. highlights.content: UPDATED 20:55 EDT / OCTOBER 23 2026 ### Moonshot AI launches new flagship Kim K3.1 Pro model with 3T parameters Moonshot AI today introduced Kim K3.1 Pro, a large language model that can perform some tasks better than Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. The LLM is a post-trained, or upgraded, version of an algorithm that the Chinese artificial intelligence company released in July. The latter model, Kimi K3, comprises 896 individual neural networks with 3 trillion parameters. It only activates 16 of those neural networks at any given time to minimize inference costs. Moonshot AI also optimizes its models’ hardware footprint in other ways. Kim K3 features Kimi Delta Attention, a custom implementation of a memory-saving technology called Gated DeltaNet. It reduces the amount of RAM that the model’s attention mechanism uses to interpret user prompts. The feature was presumably carried over to Kim K3.1 Pro. The company says the new model’s post-training workflow consumed significantly more processing power than similar projects it completed in the past. Additionally, it ran on an upgraded version of the company’s post-training stack. Moonshot AI added automated quality checks and boosted the underlying infrastructure’s efficiency. One area where Kimi K3.1 Pro delivers particularly competitive output quality is 3D modeling. There are two ways to create a 3D model of an object: engineers can draw it or they can write a code snippet that specifies its geometry in numerical terms. Kimi K3.1 Pro takes the latter approach. The LLM scored 92.7% on a 3D model coding benchmark called BenchCAD, which put it within four percentage points of Astra and Claude Opus 5.5. Kimi K3.1 Pro can not only generate static 3D models but also animate them. In one test, Moonshot AI used the model to generate an animated simulation of human motion. Another internal evaluation saw the company create multiple 3D video games. Games are difficult for AI models to generate because they contain a large amount of code and even a single bug can crash them. Pro scored 65.7% on the industry standard Terminal-Bench 4.0 coding benchmark, which put it more than 7% ahead of Astra but slightly behind Opus 5.5. Furthermore, it managed to outperform both models on OfficeQA Pro v2. It’s a test that measures LLMs’ ability to perform complex financial analysis tasks. The model’s performance on popular cybersecurity benchmarks significantly trails the scores of Astra and Opus 5.5. According to Moonshot AI, its engineers deliberately removed cybersecurity-related information from the model’s post-training dataset to address safety risks. The company plans to equip its future models with more advanced vulnerability analysis features. Kimi K3.1 Pro is available via Moonshot AI’s paid cloud services on launch. highlights.content: ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)![](https://www.elektormagazine.com/waitress/takeaway/270/image) ![llm-d 1.0 Targets Lower AI Inference Costs](https://cdn.eenewseurope.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Copy-of-Copy-of-Article-Image-Template-2026-10-22T092241.444-scaled-800x600-c-default.png) # llm-d 1.0 Targets Lower AI Inference Costs News | By Glaucileine Vieira [open source](/en/tags/open-source/) [LLM](/en/tags/llm-2/) [AI](/en/tags/ai/) [Data Centers](/en/tags/data-centers-2/) --- Running large AI models is expensive, especially when thousands of requests compete for computing resources. The open-source llm-d project aims to tackle that problem with version 1.0, introducing new capabilities for managing [AI](https://www.eenewseurope.com/en/tags/ai) inference across distributed infrastructure. Founded by Red Hat, IBM, Google Cloud, CoreWeave, and NVIDIA, the project is now governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF). For *eeNews Europe* readers, the release is particularly relevant to companies developing AI infrastructure and deploying large language models. It offers ways to improve GPU utilization, manage demanding workloads, and reduce the cost of running AI applications. ## AI Inference Gets More Efficient One of the biggest challenges in AI inference is managing the information models need to process and reuse. This becomes especially demanding with AI agents, which often handle long conversations, access large amounts of context, and run multiple tasks simultaneously. llm-d addresses these challenges through techniques such as cache-aware routing, memory offloading, and separating the processing of input prompts from generating responses. Version 1.0 adds improved workload scheduling, allowing different users and applications to share computing resources without overwhelming the system. It also introduces high-availability routing and coordinated updates, helping operators maintain services during maintenance. ## Lower Costs on Existing GPUs Recent demonstrations show what these improvements could mean for large AI deployments. In one benchmark, researchers used llm-d to run GLM 5.2, an open-weight model with approximately 753 billion parameters, on NVIDIA GPUs. The system delivered more than 6.6 million output tokens per minute at peak and supported up to 3,000 concurrent coding agents without preemptions. Based on current cloud rental rates, the researchers estimated inference costs five to ten times lower per token than comparable commercial API pricing for the tested workloads. Another project at IBM Research used open models and llm-d to investigate quantum error correction hardware. Researchers reported inference costs 11.5 times lower than an entirely proprietary configuration, with a cache hit rate of approximately 98%. These results come from specific workloads and configurations, rather than general performance guarantees. ## Built for Production AI Workloads Beyond performance, llm-d 1.0 focuses on making distributed AI inference easier to operate in production environments. The release introduces multi-tenant quality of service, session-aware routing, and support for updates without planned downtime. The project now includes more than 500 contributors from over 25 organizations. “As organizations move beyond AI experimentation and into full-scale production, the bottleneck shifts from generating answers to managing the economics, operational reliability, and extreme infrastructure demands of complex agentic workloads,” said Brian Stevens, senior vice president and AI chief technology officer at ...

[Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## Best Open Source LLM in October 2026: The Short Answer Kimi K3 is the strongest open-weight model you can download today, judging by what Moonshot AI has published: a [2.8-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts design with native vision and a 1-million-token context window](https://platform.kimi.ai/docs/guide/kimi-k3-quickstart). The full weights, model card and serving guidance landed on Hugging Face on July 27, 2026, eleven days after the July 16 launch. It is not the cheapest model here, the smallest, or the most permissively licensed. It is the one with the biggest documented ceiling. Four rivals make the best open source LLM question harder than any single leaderboard can settle. GLM-5.3 from Z.ai is the current flagship of a family that now stretches down to cheap Flash tiers. DeepSeek V4.1-Flash, refreshed on October 17 as V4.1-Flash-1017, undercuts nearly everyone on price. Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 line pairs a hosted Max flagship with open checkpoints that differ by size and license. highlights.content: ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)![](https://www.elektormagazine.com/waitress/takeaway/270/image) ![llm-d 1.0 Targets Lower AI Inference Costs](https://cdn.eenewseurope.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Copy-of-Copy-of-Article-Image-Template-2026-10-22T092241.444-scaled-800x600-c-default.png) # llm-d 1.0 Targets Lower AI Inference Costs News | By Glaucileine Vieira [open source](/en/tags/open-source/) [LLM](/en/tags/llm-2/) [AI](/en/tags/ai/) [Data Centers](/en/tags/data-centers-2/) --- Running large AI models is expensive, especially when thousands of requests compete for computing resources. The open-source llm-d project aims to tackle that problem with version 1.0, introducing new capabilities for managing [AI](https://www.eenewseurope.com/en/tags/ai) inference across distributed infrastructure. Founded by Red Hat, IBM, Google Cloud, CoreWeave, and NVIDIA, the project is now governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF). For *eeNews Europe* readers, the release is particularly relevant to companies developing AI infrastructure and deploying large language models. It offers ways to improve GPU utilization, manage demanding workloads, and reduce the cost of running AI applications. ## AI Inference Gets More Efficient One of the biggest challenges in AI inference is managing the information models need to process and reuse. This becomes especially demanding with AI agents, which often handle long conversations, access large amounts of context, and run multiple tasks simultaneously. llm-d addresses these challenges through techniques such as cache-aware routing, memory offloading, and separating the processing of input prompts from generating responses. Version 1.0 adds improved workload scheduling, allowing different users and applications to share computing resources without overwhelming the system. It also introduces high-availability routing and coordinated updates, helping operators maintain services during maintenance. ## Lower Costs on Existing GPUs Recent demonstrations show what these improvements could mean for large AI deployments. In one benchmark, researchers used llm-d to run GLM 5.2, an open-weight model with approximately 753 billion parameters, on NVIDIA GPUs. The system delivered more than 6.6 million output tokens per minute at peak and supported up to 3,000 concurrent coding agents without preemptions. Based on current cloud rental rates, the researchers estimated inference costs five to ten times lower per token than comparable commercial API pricing for the tested workloads. Another project at IBM Research used open models and llm-d to investigate quantum error correction hardware. Researchers reported inference costs 11.5 times lower than an entirely proprietary configuration, with a cache hit rate of approximately 98%. These results come from specific workloads and configurations, rather than general performance guarantees. ## Built for Production AI Workloads Beyond performance, llm-d 1.0 focuses on making distributed AI inference easier to operate in production environments. The release introduces multi-tenant quality of service, session-aware routing, and support for updates without planned downtime. The project now includes more than 500 contributors from over 25 organizations. “As organizations move beyond AI experimentation and into full-scale production, the bottleneck shifts from generating answers to managing the economics, operational reliability, and extreme infrastructure demands of complex agentic workloads,” said Brian Stevens, senior vice president and AI chief technology officer at ...

The company is warning that agents don't need to be hacked or deliberately turned malicious to cause problems. That's not to say AI agents are suddenly running amok across businesses. Rather, Microsoft is concerned about how much freedom organizations are giving them, particularly when they can access sensitive data and make decisions without human approval. Its proposed solution is to use Guardian Agents to monitor their counterparts, adding another layer of oversight to increasingly autonomous systems. Elsewhere this week, Microsoft's October Windows updates are causing problems for Exchange Server deployments, with administrators reporting email disruption and database availability issues. At the same time, new cybersecurity jobs data points to a contracting market, even as demand for AI Security Engineers and Cyber Data Scientists rises sharply. These developments raise different questions about keeping critical business systems running and how cybersecurity skills demand is changing. ## Microsoft Warns AI Agents Could Become Insider Threats Microsoft is urging organizations to treat AI agents as potential insider threats, warning that systems with access to sensitive data and business-critical tools can cause harm without being deliberately compromised. The company published its latest guidance on October 19, arguing that security controls must account for agents that [behave unpredictably](https://uctoday.com/openai-just-went-rogue-and-cyber-attacked-a-startup) as their tasks and surrounding context change. **Microsoft Chairman and CEO Satya Nadella** argues that organizations should separate a model's intelligence from its authority, saying: > “The most trustworthy agentic system will not be the one with the model we trust most. It will be the one designed that enables us to trust the model least.” In practice, that means the model should not control the security boundaries governing its own access or actions. As Nadella explained, the most trustworthy systems are those designed to operate within external constraints, rather than relying on confidence in the model itself. The company is proposing Guardian Agents to monitor other agents, assess changing risk and intervene when necessary. This builds on Project Perception, introduced in July, which combines enterprise security signals with specialized red, blue and green agents to identify weaknesses, investigate threats and help remediate problems. Microsoft is now extending that approach to the risks posed by agents operating inside organizations. ## Exchange Server Instability Follows October Windows Updates Microsoft has acknowledged reports that October's Windows Server updates are causing instability in some Exchange Server environments. AI Agents.content: [![UC Today](/_next/image?url=%2Fbrand%2Fuc-today-logo.png&w=1920&q=75)powering productive workplaces](/) [Front page](/) News[Trust & Risk](/beat/trust-risk)15h · 09:01 BST · 4 min read # AI Agent Risks, Exchange Issues and a Shifting Cyber Market Microsoft is warning that autonomous AI agents could create insider threats, while October Windows updates are disrupting some Exchange Server environments and US cybersecurity job postings are falling despite sharp growth in demand for specialist AI security roles, highlighting the operational and ![](/_next/image?url=https%3A%2F%2Fjrueuulzybfnqbgsdwwt.supabase.co%2Fstorage%2Fv1%2Fobject%2Fpublic%2Favatars%2F3b8ec3f4-d7e8-43c3-9dc6-e95bb2de1c58%2Favatar.jfif%3Fv%3D1787131806280&w=3840&q=75)[Kristian McCann](/author/kristian-mccann) For a while now, AI agents have been a growing source of cybersecurity concern, but this week Microsoft has raised an uncomfortable question: what happens when the technology you're relying on to get work done becomes a security risk itself? The company is warning that agents don't need to be hacked or deliberately turned malicious to cause problems. That's not to say AI agents are suddenly running amok across businesses. Rather, Microsoft is concerned about how much freedom organizations are giving them, particularly when they can access sensitive data and make decisions without human approval. AI Agents.content: # You gave your AI agent access, but who is giving it orders? ###### Gen Digital * October 23, 2026 * 10:00 AM * 0 Headlines warn that AI could threaten humanity, and it’s easy to wave that off as science fiction. But the real danger is more ordinary and already here. Research published by Gen Threat Labs demonstrated how quickly an AI agent’s autonomy can become a liability. In a controlled experiment, researchers manipulated an agent through content it encountered while reading email, prompting it to execute system commands, transmit data outside its environment and perform destructive file operations. No software vulnerability was required. The agent simply treated untrusted content as instruction. That autonomy is expanding daily. Agents are moving from answering questions to taking action doing everything from executing code, connecting to services, managing files and making decisions on a user’s behalf. The shift from developer-focused tools like OpenClaw to widespread use of personal assistants like Muse, happened quickly. Delegating work across platforms is becoming commonplace and how people interact with AI. The risks extend beyond manipulating agents. In October, Gen Threat Labs documented Warden Stealer, malware targeting configuration files and local data associated with AI assistants and coding tools, potentially exposing credentials, access tokens and conversation histories. When software can act with a user’s permissions, trust can’t be reduced to whether a model produces a safe-sounding answer. People need to know what an agent can access, where it is connecting, what it is doing and whether the protection around it works. That is why Gen is building the Agent Trust Hub: a trust layer designed to extend protection across the agent lifecycle, from verification and visibility to runtime safety and enforcement. ## Trust starts before an agent acts Agentic systems gain capabilities through skills, plugins, tools and other integrations. These extensions make agents more useful, but they also expand risk by introducing hidden instructions, excessive permissions, and malicious code. Earlier this year, Gen researchers identified that 12% of skills available on ClawHub – at the time – were malicious. Many impersonated legitimate extensions while introducing instructions designed to trick agents into downloading malware. The Agent Trust Hub (ATH) helps assess these risks before a capability is installed or used. It brings together skill scanning, a curated marketplace of trusted skills and mechanisms that allow agents to check themselves for safety. Gen’s partnership with Vercel also brings verification and visible risk ratings into the skills.sh ecosystem, where developers discover and install new capabilities. ## Securing how agents connect Agents communicate across services, regions and websites, often at a speed and scale that traditional human-oriented controls were not designed to manage. VPN for Agents, a part of the ATH, addresses that connectivity gap with an AI-native VPN built for autonomous agents. Powered by Norton VPN infrastructure, it provides encrypted, private connectivity without requiring a conventional client installation. Its multi-tunnel design allows multiple agents to operate simultaneously through separate protected connections, including across different countries. The architecture gives people greater control over how agents communicate and helps protect an agent’s identity and location while it works. ## Use AI Agents Safely with Gen's Agent Trust Hub AI agents can install skills and take action on your behalf, which makes a single compromised skill a security risk. Gen’s Agent Trust Hub provides free tools that scan skills before installation and let you control what your agents can access. LLMs.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # ResCity-LLM Pipeline Turns Urban Resilience Knowledge Into Specialized AI Models ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=80&r=g) ![ResCity-LLM Pipeline Turns Urban Resilience Knowledge Into Specialized AI Models](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/stackrss-featured-14422-750x422.png) ResCity-LLM Pipeline Turns Urban Resilience Knowledge Into Specialized AI Models A team of urban resilience and earthquake engineering researchers has unveiled a complete pipeline for building large language models that can absorb the sprawling, fragmented knowledge of resilient cities and then deploy it across professional disaster-prevention tasks. The framework, called ResCity-LLM, links together four stages that had previously existed in isolation: assembling a domain corpus, generating training data automatically, adapting open-source models through a two-stage training strategy, and evaluating the results on a purpose-built benchmark. When the strongest adapted model was tested against two much larger general-purpose systems, it came out ahead on the benchmark’s overall weighted score, offering early evidence that compact, locally deployable models can compete with cloud giants in a specialized engineering domain. The motivation stems from an uncomfortable mismatch between what urban resilience research demands and what general-purpose language models are trained to do. Urban resilience draws on engineering, environment, planning, ecology, economics, sociology and governance simultaneously, with relevant knowledge scattered across academic papers, technical standards, planning documents, policy texts and case studies. General-purpose models such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek and Claude are trained overwhelmingly on general text, so they struggle to cover the complex knowledge structures, specialized semantics and typical task scenarios of this interdisciplinary field. Unlike medicine or law, where domain-specific language model research is relatively mature, resilience-oriented work had remained scattered and exploratory, lacking a systematic framework that spans corpus organization, training data construction, model training and specialized benchmark evaluation. The first ingredient is a data foundation the researchers call ResCity-Corpus. Using keywords related to urban and resilient cities in both English and Chinese, the team harvested academic literature from Elsevier, Nature, Springer, arXiv and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure, crawled news reports from mainstream media platforms, and collected professional monographs together with national, industry and local technical standards covering disaster prevention, urban lifeline systems and related fields. The final processed corpus for continued pre-training contained 60,059 text blocks amounting to 96.80 million tokens, split roughly 69 percent English and 31 percent Chinese, and organized into seven thematic categories ranging from hazard and climate science to governance and public policy. Raw corpora of this kind are notoriously messy, so the researchers designed what they call a multi-agent collaborative dual-stage data generation pipeline. In the first stage, aimed at continued pre-training, a clean-agent parses heterogeneous documents and strips out noise, a chunk-agent segments long texts into semantically coherent units sized by tokenizer length with overlapping tails to preserve context, a quality-agent powered by a commercial language model scores each chunk and flags low-quality or incomplete samples, and a repair-agent performs minimal fixes to broken sentences and grammatical errors without altering the underlying knowledge content. LLMs.content: UPDATED 20:55 EDT / OCTOBER 23 2026 ### Moonshot AI launches new flagship Kim K3.1 Pro model with 3T parameters Moonshot AI today introduced Kim K3.1 Pro, a large language model that can perform some tasks better than Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. The LLM is a post-trained, or upgraded, version of an algorithm that the Chinese artificial intelligence company released in July. The latter model, Kimi K3, comprises 896 individual neural networks with 3 trillion parameters. It only activates 16 of those neural networks at any given time to minimize inference costs. Moonshot AI also optimizes its models’ hardware footprint in other ways. Kim K3 features Kimi Delta Attention, a custom implementation of a memory-saving technology called Gated DeltaNet. It reduces the amount of RAM that the model’s attention mechanism uses to interpret user prompts. The feature was presumably carried over to Kim K3.1 Pro. The company says the new model’s post-training workflow consumed significantly more processing power than similar projects it completed in the past. Additionally, it ran on an upgraded version of the company’s post-training stack. Moonshot AI added automated quality checks and boosted the underlying infrastructure’s efficiency. One area where Kimi K3.1 Pro delivers particularly competitive output quality is 3D modeling. There are two ways to create a 3D model of an object: engineers can draw it or they can write a code snippet that specifies its geometry in numerical terms. Kimi K3.1 Pro takes the latter approach. The LLM scored 92.7% on a 3D model coding benchmark called BenchCAD, which put it within four percentage points of Astra and Claude Opus 5.5. Kimi K3.1 Pro can not only generate static 3D models but also animate them. In one test, Moonshot AI used the model to generate an animated simulation of human motion. Another internal evaluation saw the company create multiple 3D video games. Games are difficult for AI models to generate because they contain a large amount of code and even a single bug can crash them. Pro scored 65.7% on the industry standard Terminal-Bench 4.0 coding benchmark, which put it more than 7% ahead of Astra but slightly behind Opus 5.5. Furthermore, it managed to outperform both models on OfficeQA Pro v2. It’s a test that measures LLMs’ ability to perform complex financial analysis tasks. The model’s performance on popular cybersecurity benchmarks significantly trails the scores of Astra and Opus 5.5. According to Moonshot AI, its engineers deliberately removed cybersecurity-related information from the model’s post-training dataset to address safety risks. The company plans to equip its future models with more advanced vulnerability analysis features. Kimi K3.1 Pro is available via Moonshot AI’s paid cloud services on launch. The company plans to open-source the model’s weights by Nov. 4. ##### Image: Unsplash # A message from John Furrier, co-founder of SiliconANGLE: Support our mission to keep content open and free by engaging with theCUBE community. LLMs.content: ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)![](https://www.elektormagazine.com/waitress/takeaway/270/image) ![llm-d 1.0 Targets Lower AI Inference Costs](https://cdn.eenewseurope.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Copy-of-Copy-of-Article-Image-Template-2026-10-22T092241.444-scaled-800x600-c-default.png) # llm-d 1.0 Targets Lower AI Inference Costs News | By Glaucileine Vieira [open source](/en/tags/open-source/) [LLM](/en/tags/llm-2/) [AI](/en/tags/ai/) [Data Centers](/en/tags/data-centers-2/) --- Running large AI models is expensive, especially when thousands of requests compete for computing resources. The open-source llm-d project aims to tackle that problem with version 1.0, introducing new capabilities for managing [AI](https://www.eenewseurope.com/en/tags/ai) inference across distributed infrastructure. Founded by Red Hat, IBM, Google Cloud, CoreWeave, and NVIDIA, the project is now governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF). For *eeNews Europe* readers, the release is particularly relevant to companies developing AI infrastructure and deploying large language models. It offers ways to improve GPU utilization, manage demanding workloads, and reduce the cost of running AI applications. ## AI Inference Gets More Efficient One of the biggest challenges in AI inference is managing the information models need to process and reuse. This becomes especially demanding with AI agents, which often handle long conversations, access large amounts of context, and run multiple tasks simultaneously. llm-d addresses these challenges through techniques such as cache-aware routing, memory offloading, and separating the processing of input prompts from generating responses. Version 1.0 adds improved workload scheduling, allowing different users and applications to share computing resources without overwhelming the system. It also introduces high-availability routing and coordinated updates, helping operators maintain services during maintenance. ## Lower Costs on Existing GPUs Recent demonstrations show what these improvements could mean for large AI deployments. In one benchmark, researchers used llm-d to run GLM 5.2, an open-weight model with approximately 753 billion parameters, on NVIDIA GPUs. The system delivered more than 6.6 million output tokens per minute at peak and supported up to 3,000 concurrent coding agents without preemptions. Based on current cloud rental rates, the researchers estimated inference costs five to ten times lower per token than comparable commercial API pricing for the tested workloads. Another project at IBM Research used open models and llm-d to investigate quantum error correction hardware. Researchers reported inference costs 11.5 times lower than an entirely proprietary configuration, with a cache hit rate of approximately 98%. These results come from specific workloads and configurations, rather than general performance guarantees. ## Built for Production AI Workloads Beyond performance, llm-d 1.0 focuses on making distributed AI inference easier to operate in production environments. The release introduces multi-tenant quality of service, session-aware routing, and support for updates without planned downtime. The project now includes more than 500 contributors from over 25 organizations. “As organizations move beyond AI experimentation and into full-scale production, the bottleneck shifts from generating answers to managing the economics, operational reliability, and extreme infrastructure demands of complex agentic workloads,” said Brian Stevens, senior vice president and AI chief technology officer at ...

[Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## Best Open Source LLM in October 2026: The Short Answer Kimi K3 is the strongest open-weight model you can download today, judging by what Moonshot AI has published: a [2.8-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts design with native vision and a 1-million-token context window](https://platform.kimi.ai/docs/guide/kimi-k3-quickstart). The full weights, model card and serving guidance landed on Hugging Face on July 27, 2026, eleven days after the July 16 launch. It is not the cheapest model here, the smallest, or the most permissively licensed. It is the one with the biggest documented ceiling. Four rivals make the best open source LLM question harder than any single leaderboard can settle. GLM-5.3 from Z.ai is the current flagship of a family that now stretches down to cheap Flash tiers. DeepSeek V4.1-Flash, refreshed on October 17 as V4.1-Flash-1017, undercuts nearly everyone on price. Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 line pairs a hosted Max flagship with open checkpoints that differ by size and license. Mistral Large 4 sits in public preview, with weights promised by the end of October but not downloadable on October 23. The field moves weekly. [Kimi K3’s run on a coding leaderboard](https://shattered.io/kimi-k3-coding-leaderboard-2026/) earlier this month put Chinese open-weight labs in the spotlight, and a stream of releases since then has crowded the shortlist. Specs, license terms, published benchmarks, per-token prices, hardware needs and migration effort all point in slightly different directions, so the right winner depends on what you plan to build. ### Quick picks by priority * **Highest documented ceiling:** Kimi K3, with open weights, 2.8T parameters and a 1M-token window. * **Lowest price per token:** DeepSeek V4.1-Flash at $0.15 input and $0.60 output off-peak, with GLM-5.3-Flash close behind at $0.15 input and $0.50 output. * **Best fit for one workstation GPU:** the Qwen3.8 27B dense checkpoint, which secondary reports tie to an Apache 2.0 license. * **Best for agentic coding and security work:** GLM-5.3, based on Z.ai’s own claims. * **Best bet for European data residency:** Mistral Large 4, once its weights and license actually ship. ### What is confirmed and what is not Treat every vendor-reported benchmark as a claim until an independent leaderboard repeats it. No head-to-head test covering all five models existed on October 23, 2026, and several of the numbers below come from the labs themselves. Where a figure rests on one report, the wording says “reportedly” or names the outlet. Where a successor is announced but unreleased, such as DeepSeek V4.1-Pro or Alibaba’s Qwen 4, it gets one sentence and no invented dates. ## Open Source vs Open Weight: What Each License Really Allows Almost none of the models people call open source LLMs meet the strict definition. You get the trained weights and usually a model card, but not the training data, the full training code or the right to do anything you like. Open weight is the accurate label, and the license attached to those weights decides whether a startup, a bank or a government contractor can ship a product on top of them. Kimi K3 shows the pattern clearly. Moonshot published the weights under a custom Kimi K3 License, and coverage of the release is explicit that it should not be described as MIT or Apache 2.0. Why founders keep failing to vibecode their own LLM inference engine A University of Washington project called VibeServe needed a multi-agent research pipeline, not a few prompts, to make AI-written inference engines match vLLM, exposing why founders chasing cheaper compute keep hitting a wall. ![](https://startupfortune.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/08/davepress.png) [Dave Barr](https://startupfortune.com/author/dave/) · 6 min read · 637 reads ![Why founders keep failing to vibecode their own LLM inference engine](https://startupfortune.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/vllm-vibeserve-fireworks-ai-1024x576.jpg) *Coding assistants can write almost any function on command, but a growing number of founders are learning that an LLM inference engine is not a function, it's a systems problem, and the gap between the two is where their cost-cutting plans go to die.* Ask Claude Code or Cursor to write a Python script and you'll likely get something that runs. Ask the same tools to build a serving stack that runs a large language model efficiently at scale, and you'll likely get something that compiles, loads a model, and then falls over the moment real traffic hits it. That's the uncomfortable discovery playing out across AI builder communities right now. It has a name in the research literature: the gap between agentic code generation and actual systems engineering. The clearest evidence isn't anecdotal. In May 2026, researchers at the University of Washington published VibeServe, a project built specifically to test whether AI agents could synthesize a complete LLM serving runtime, the scheduler, the memory manager, the batching logic, the kernel selection, from scratch. VibeServe used a two-loop architecture, according to the project's writeup on the university's Systems and Data Science lab blog. An outer loop plans and searches across possible system designs. An inner loop implements each candidate, checks it for correctness, and benchmarks it against the target workload. Across six case studies, the system matched the performance of vLLM and SGLang, two of the most heavily optimized open-source inference engines, on mainstream deployments. AI Product.content: IT Brief Asia - Technology news for CIOs & IT decision-makers [![IT Brief Asia logo](/brands/itb-new-logo.svg)](/) [Powered By ![TechDay logo](/brands/td-new-logo-right.svg)](https://techday.asia) ![ABBYY launches PHOENIX Plus for document automation](https://itbrief.asia/uploads/story/2026/10/24/enterprise-document-automation-workflow-pipeline-ai-illustration-story-322271.webp) [Risk & Compliance](https://itbrief.asia/tag/risk-compliance) [ERP](https://itbrief.asia/tag/enterprise-resource-planning) [GenAI](https://itbrief.asia/tag/generative-ai) # ABBYY launches PHOENIX Plus for document automation Fri, 23rd Oct 2026 (Yesterday) [![Sofiah Nichole Salivio](https://itbrief.asia/rails/active_storage/representations/redirect/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6MTYyNywicHVyIjoiYmxvYl9pZCJ9fQ==--3f3cbcdb3f86206827b894ccc07566b24a1d49e6/eyJfcmFpbHMiOnsiZGF0YSI6eyJmb3JtYXQiOiJ3ZWJwIiwicmVzaXplX3RvX2ZpbGwiOlsxNjAsMTYwXSwicXVhbGl0eSI6ODV9LCJwdXIiOiJ2YXJpYXRpb24ifX0=--89ddf5e6765c65a563c2258053e9d33c05d195da/unnamed%20(2).webp) SOFIAH NICHOLE SALIVIO News Editor](/author/sofiah-nichole-salivio) ABBYY has launched PHOENIX Plus, a generative AI layer for its Vantage document processing platform aimed at organisations using automation to handle business documents. Built into Vantage, the new layer is designed to improve how software extracts and interprets information from complex files, including documents with varied formats, handwritten content and unstructured text. It turns documents into structured data for use in automated workflows and AI systems. The launch comes as companies try to deploy AI agents more widely across back-office tasks while still struggling with the variability of contracts, forms and other operational records. Document handling remains a constraint for many automation projects because systems must first read and classify information accurately before acting on it. PHOENIX Plus is part of ABBYY's broader PHOENIX portfolio, which combines deterministic AI tools with generative models. Within that structure, PHOENIX Core provides the optical character recognition, layout analysis, classification and extraction functions that have long underpinned the company's document software. PHOENIX Plus adds generative AI for less predictable document types and more interpretive tasks. One intended use is zero-shot extraction for unseen or highly variable documents, where users define the output they need through prompts rather than labelled training data. This could apply to files such as supplier contracts, where layout, language and clause structure differ widely and often require manual review before important information can be pulled into compliance or contract management systems. The software also supports tasks beyond extraction, including interpreting free-form text, identifying inconsistencies and producing recommendations for downstream decisions. Those features are designed to sit alongside existing validation rules, confidence thresholds, human review processes and source traceability within Vantage. **Hybrid approach** ABBYY is positioning the product around a hybrid model, arguing that deterministic techniques remain important where consistency and precision are required, while generative AI is better suited to ambiguity and reasoning. That framing reflects a broader trend in enterprise software, where suppliers are trying to blend large language models with established automation tools rather than replace them outright. PHOENIX Plus is hosted by ABBYY and keeps customer data within the same region as the user's Vantage data. Customers can buy the software as an add-on to their Vantage subscription for a fixed annual fee, rather than entering a separate contract with a model provider or managing token-based billing. At the same time, users can still connect Vantage to external model providers through a bring-your-own-model option. AI Product.content: By: [Robert Ambrogi](https://www.lawnext.com/) [![Robert Ambrogi](https://justatic.com/v/20250319a/external/lawsitesblog/images/logo.png) Robert Ambrogi Blog](https://www.lawnext.com/) # Conseal, a New On-Device Privacy App, Masks Sensitive Client Data Before It Reaches AI Tools Like ChatGPT and Claude ![Conseal, a New On-Device Privacy App, Masks Sensitive Client Data Before It Reaches AI Tools Like ChatGPT and Claude](https://www.lawnext.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/conseal-lnpr_lawnextpr.png) By [Sprintfour](https://www.lawnext.com/author/sprintfour) on Tweet ![twitter]() Share ![linkedin]() Share ![facebook]() *7 in 10 lawyers at law firms work solo or in firms of 10 or fewer, where the enterprise AI plans large firms use to protect client confidentiality are largely out of reach.* **MIAMI, FL | October 23, 2026.** Sprintfour Technologies today announced the public launch of Conseal, a desktop application for Windows and macOS that detects and removes sensitive information entirely on the user’s own computer, both in documents and in real time as users type in any application. Conseal lets lawyers redact or anonymize client details before sharing them with AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude, and the data never leaves their device. #### **Small Firms, Same Obligations** AI tools have made it easy to paste a client file into a chat window. For lawyers, that convenience runs straight into the duty of confidentiality. ABA Model Rule 1.6(c) requires lawyers to make reasonable efforts to prevent unauthorized disclosure of client information, and ABA Formal Opinion 512 asks lawyers to weigh the disclosure risk before entering client information into generative AI tools. That responsibility extends to the paralegals and staff who handle client documents every day, since Model Rule 5.3 makes lawyers accountable for how their team handles client information. Most of the lawyers facing this question work at small firms. According to American Bar Association data, 7 in 10 lawyers at law firms work solo or in firms of 10 or fewer, roughly 700,000 attorneys. They answer to the same rules as Big Law, but without an enterprise security team behind them, and the enterprise AI plans and private deployments that large firms rely on are largely out of their reach. Data masking and de-identification tools were built for enterprises. The small business tools that exist are mostly redaction tools that support only a few file formats, whether cloud or local. Tools that run completely on the user’s device and anonymize data in a way that preserves its meaning for AI are still a gap in the market. Conseal fills that gap. It is built around the individual practitioner, letting lawyers mask and de-identify client data before sharing it with external AI. “I ran into this problem while building another AI tool,” said **Ash Malepati, founder and CEO of Sprintfour**. “Professionals wanted to use it, but they didn’t trust uploading confidential client information to a third-party AI, and they were right to. Stripping out identifying details by hand took hours, and every alternative either sent data to a third-party cloud, missed too much, or was limited to redaction in a few formats. We designed Conseal from the bottom up, putting the technology in the hands of each individual, right on their own computer. We’re starting in the legal industry because that’s where we heard the need the loudest.” #### **How Conseal Works** Conseal runs lightweight AI models directly on the user’s computer. Detection, redaction and anonymization all happen locally. The app connects to the internet only to validate the license and check for updates, and never transmits document content or anything users type. Conseal includes: * **Redact:** permanently removes sensitive information for court filings and discovery productions. Lawyers who mark redactions item by item in Adobe Acrobat today can cut that work from hours to minutes. * **Anonymize:** replaces sensitive details ...

Data masking and de-identification tools were built for enterprises. The small business tools that exist are mostly redaction tools that support only a few file formats, whether cloud or local. Tools that run completely on the user’s device and anonymize data in a way that preserves its meaning for AI are still a gap in the market. Conseal fills that gap. We’re starting in the legal industry because that’s where we heard the need the loudest.” #### **How Conseal Works** Conseal runs lightweight AI models directly on the user’s computer. Open Source AI.content: ![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)![](https://www.elektormagazine.com/waitress/takeaway/270/image) ![llm-d 1.0 Targets Lower AI Inference Costs](https://cdn.eenewseurope.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Copy-of-Copy-of-Article-Image-Template-2026-10-22T092241.444-scaled-800x600-c-default.png) # llm-d 1.0 Targets Lower AI Inference Costs News | By Glaucileine Vieira [open source](/en/tags/open-source/) [LLM](/en/tags/llm-2/) [AI](/en/tags/ai/) [Data Centers](/en/tags/data-centers-2/) --- Running large AI models is expensive, especially when thousands of requests compete for computing resources. The open-source llm-d project aims to tackle that problem with version 1.0, introducing new capabilities for managing [AI](https://www.eenewseurope.com/en/tags/ai) inference across distributed infrastructure. Founded by Red Hat, IBM, Google Cloud, CoreWeave, and NVIDIA, the project is now governed by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF). For *eeNews Europe* readers, the release is particularly relevant to companies developing AI infrastructure and deploying large language models. It offers ways to improve GPU utilization, manage demanding workloads, and reduce the cost of running AI applications. ## AI Inference Gets More Efficient One of the biggest challenges in AI inference is managing the information models need to process and reuse. This becomes especially demanding with AI agents, which often handle long conversations, access large amounts of context, and run multiple tasks simultaneously. llm-d addresses these challenges through techniques such as cache-aware routing, memory offloading, and separating the processing of input prompts from generating responses. Version 1.0 adds improved workload scheduling, allowing different users and applications to share computing resources without overwhelming the system. It also introduces high-availability routing and coordinated updates, helping operators maintain services during maintenance. ## Lower Costs on Existing GPUs Recent demonstrations show what these improvements could mean for large AI deployments. In one benchmark, researchers used llm-d to run GLM 5.2, an open-weight model with approximately 753 billion parameters, on NVIDIA GPUs. The system delivered more than 6.6 million output tokens per minute at peak and supported up to 3,000 concurrent coding agents without preemptions. Based on current cloud rental rates, the researchers estimated inference costs five to ten times lower per token than comparable commercial API pricing for the tested workloads. Another project at IBM Research used open models and llm-d to investigate quantum error correction hardware. Researchers reported inference costs 11.5 times lower than an entirely proprietary configuration, with a cache hit rate of approximately 98%. These results come from specific workloads and configurations, rather than general performance guarantees. ## Built for Production AI Workloads Beyond performance, llm-d 1.0 focuses on making distributed AI inference easier to operate in production environments. The release introduces multi-tenant quality of service, session-aware routing, and support for updates without planned downtime. [Add now](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?hl=en&q=https%3A%2F%2Fshattered.io%2F) ## Best Open Source LLM in October 2026: The Short Answer Kimi K3 is the strongest open-weight model you can download today, judging by what Moonshot AI has published: a [2.8-trillion-parameter mixture-of-experts design with native vision and a 1-million-token context window](https://platform.kimi.ai/docs/guide/kimi-k3-quickstart). The full weights, model card and serving guidance landed on Hugging Face on July 27, 2026, eleven days after the July 16 launch. It is not the cheapest model here, the smallest, or the most permissively licensed. It is the one with the biggest documented ceiling. Four rivals make the best open source LLM question harder than any single leaderboard can settle. GLM-5.3 from Z.ai is the current flagship of a family that now stretches down to cheap Flash tiers. DeepSeek V4.1-Flash, refreshed on October 17 as V4.1-Flash-1017, undercuts nearly everyone on price. Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 line pairs a hosted Max flagship with open checkpoints that differ by size and license. Mistral Large 4 sits in public preview, with weights promised by the end of October but not downloadable on October 23. The field moves weekly. [Kimi K3’s run on a coding leaderboard](https://shattered.io/kimi-k3-coding-leaderboard-2026/) earlier this month put Chinese open-weight labs in the spotlight, and a stream of releases since then has crowded the shortlist. Specs, license terms, published benchmarks, per-token prices, hardware needs and migration effort all point in slightly different directions, so the right winner depends on what you plan to build. ### Quick picks by priority * **Highest documented ceiling:** Kimi K3, with open weights, 2.8T parameters and a 1M-token window. * **Lowest price per token:** DeepSeek V4.1-Flash at $0.15 input and $0.60 output off-peak, with GLM-5.3-Flash close behind at $0.15 input and $0.50 output. * **Best fit for one workstation GPU:** the Qwen3.8 27B dense checkpoint, which secondary reports tie to an Apache 2.0 license. * **Best for agentic coding and security work:** GLM-5.3, based on Z.ai’s own claims. * **Best bet for European data residency:** Mistral Large 4, once its weights and license actually ship. ### What is confirmed and what is not Treat every vendor-reported benchmark as a claim until an independent leaderboard repeats it. No head-to-head test covering all five models existed on October 23, 2026, and several of the numbers below come from the labs themselves. Where a figure rests on one report, the wording says “reportedly” or names the outlet. Where a successor is announced but unreleased, such as DeepSeek V4.1-Pro or Alibaba’s Qwen 4, it gets one sentence and no invented dates. ## Open Source vs Open Weight: What Each License Really Allows Almost none of the models people call open source LLMs meet the strict definition. You get the trained weights and usually a model card, but not the training data, the full training code or the right to do anything you like. Open weight is the accurate label, and the license attached to those weights decides whether a startup, a bank or a government contractor can ship a product on top of them. Open Source AI.titleZh: LiteLLM says hackers poisoned it with GitHub tokens leaked via Claude Code
Open Source AI.content: LiteLLM says hackers took the keys they needed from its own logs. They used them to publish a poisoned version of its software on Wednesday. The open-source AI gateway explained it in an incident report. Its chief executive, chief technology officer and director of security signed it. Its engineers found that Anthropic’s coding agent, Claude Code, sometimes puts a user’s GitHub command-line login token into a response. If something logs those responses, the tokens may end up in LiteLLM’s logs, the company said. > “We believe the attacker gained access to this deployment, obtained the GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from its logs, and subsequently used those credentials to compromise our release workflow,” LiteLLM wrote. The deployment was LiteLLM’s own internal one, open to the public internet. It held an “unexpected, innocuously named user account”, the company said. LiteLLM has not confirmed how the attacker got in, but suspects a recently patched vulnerability. ## Three stolen tokens LiteLLM lets developers reach many AI models through one API. The poisoned version, 1.107.0, sat on PyPI from 11:39 to 13:23 UTC on 21 October. PyPI is the main Python package index. Its Docker images were live from 11:46 to 14:20 UTC. LiteLLM said its official 1.107.0 source tag on GitHub does not contain the malicious files. Researchers at Upwind first reported the poisoned release on GitHub. LiteLLM said on X that it learned of it at 6:32am Pacific time. That was almost two hours after the release went out. The attacker held three developers’ GitHub credentials. On Monday, LiteLLM had widened release rights so two engineers could ship daily fixes for customers. The attacker used a token from one of its two GitHub organisation owners to switch off branch protection. A second developer’s credential approved the production release, which was built from a lookalike repository, Berri-AI/litellm. A third deleted the workflow records. ## Stolen keys put to use The package carried a credential stealer and a backdoor, according to the security firm Wiz. Both were set to run when Python starts. The stealer took browser passwords and cookies, cloud keys, SSH keys and API keys for AI services. It also pulled the AI provider keys stored in a LiteLLM proxy’s database. The backdoor works only on Linux and macOS. Every hour, it checked a GitHub repository for a server to fetch more code from. That repository never held more than test values, and GitHub took it down, Wiz said. It added that the malware showed strong signs of being written with AI help. Wiz cited data from ClickPy showing about 49,000 downloads of the poisoned version. About four and a half hours after the theft, Wiz saw the attacker test stolen Amazon Web Services credentials. They came from build servers and Kubernetes nodes. The checks included listing models on Amazon Bedrock. Wiz said this was consistent with LLMjacking, the use of stolen cloud access to run AI models. > “The dual-technique approach, using both .pth files and sitecustomize.py simultaneously, appears to be the first documented case in the wild,” Wiz researchers Benjamin Read and Rami McCarthy wrote. The attack landed on the same day as two critical PHP flaws. ## A second attack this year It is LiteLLM’s second compromise in 2026. In March, two poisoned versions sat on PyPI for about 40 minutes. LiteLLM traced that attack to Trivy, a security scanner in its build pipeline. Hackers also used Trivy to breach the European Commission. Mercor, an AI data firm, was hit too, and Meta froze AI data work with the company. Socket, a supply-chain security firm, told The Hacker News it had found no evidence linking the two attacks. It said the encryption keys, the way data was sent out and the backdoor all differ. > “That doesn’t rule out the same operator using different tooling, but we don’t have evidence to support that attribution,” Socket said. Open Source AI.titleZh: ResCity-LLM Pipeline Turns Urban Resilience Knowledge Into Specialized AI
Open Source AI.content: ![BIOENGINEER.ORG](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/09/logo_sariyazi.png) ![Bioengineer.org](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/11/logo352-e1516556386659.png) # ResCity-LLM Pipeline Turns Urban Resilience Knowledge Into Specialized AI Models ![](https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/?s=80&r=g) ![ResCity-LLM Pipeline Turns Urban Resilience Knowledge Into Specialized AI Models](https://bioengineer.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/stackrss-featured-14422-750x422.png) ResCity-LLM Pipeline Turns Urban Resilience Knowledge Into Specialized AI Models A team of urban resilience and earthquake engineering researchers has unveiled a complete pipeline for building large language models that can absorb the sprawling, fragmented knowledge of resilient cities and then deploy it across professional disaster-prevention tasks. The framework, called ResCity-LLM, links together four stages that had previously existed in isolation: assembling a domain corpus, generating training data automatically, adapting open-source models through a two-stage training strategy, and evaluating the results on a purpose-built benchmark. When the strongest adapted model was tested against two much larger general-purpose systems, it came out ahead on the benchmark’s overall weighted score, offering early evidence that compact, locally deployable models can compete with cloud giants in a specialized engineering domain. The motivation stems from an uncomfortable mismatch between what urban resilience research demands and what general-purpose language models are trained to do. Urban resilience draws on engineering, environment, planning, ecology, economics, sociology and governance simultaneously, with relevant knowledge scattered across academic papers, technical standards, planning documents, policy texts and case studies. General-purpose models such as ChatGPT, DeepSeek and Claude are trained overwhelmingly on general text, so they struggle to cover the complex knowledge structures, specialized semantics and typical task scenarios of this interdisciplinary field. Unlike medicine or law, where domain-specific language model research is relatively mature, resilience-oriented work had remained scattered and exploratory, lacking a systematic framework that spans corpus organization, training data construction, model training and specialized benchmark evaluation. The first ingredient is a data foundation the researchers call ResCity-Corpus. Using keywords related to urban and resilient cities in both English and Chinese, the team harvested academic literature from Elsevier, Nature, Springer, arXiv and the China National Knowledge Infrastructure, crawled news reports from mainstream media platforms, and collected professional monographs together with national, industry and local technical standards covering disaster prevention, urban lifeline systems and related fields. The final processed corpus for continued pre-training contained 60,059 text blocks amounting to 96.80 million tokens, split roughly 69 percent English and 31 percent Chinese, and organized into seven thematic categories ranging from hazard and climate science to governance and public policy. Raw corpora of this kind are notoriously messy, so the researchers designed what they call a multi-agent collaborative dual-stage data generation pipeline. In the first stage, aimed at continued pre-training, a clean-agent parses heterogeneous documents and strips out noise, a chunk-agent segments long texts into semantically coherent units sized by tokenizer length with overlapping tails to preserve context, a quality-agent powered by a commercial language model scores each chunk and flags low-quality or incomplete samples, and a repair-agent performs minimal fixes to broken sentences and grammatical errors without altering the underlying knowledge content. Infra & Chips.content: ![](https://www.techtarget.com/rms/onlineimages/ai_a264431831_searchsitetablet_520X173.jpg) your123 - stock.adobe.com # AI inference is changing data center design requirements ## AI inference requires distinct infrastructure compared to training, focusing on low latency, appropriate hardware based on workload, and tailored power and cooling methods. ![Abhishek Jadhav](https://cdn.ttgtmedia.com/rms/onlineimages/abhishek_jadhav.jpg) Much of the current expansion of AI infrastructure has focused on large GPU clusters designed to train foundation models. These deployments concentrate substantial computing resources and require high-speed interconnects, electrical capacity and advanced cooling infrastructure. But as AI applications move into production, inference introduces different [infrastructure requirements](https://www.techtarget.com/ai/tip/Planning-AI-infrastructure-upgrades-Four-steps-for-success). Inference uses trained models to process requests for enterprise assistants, customer service, document processing and automated workflows. These workloads can vary in computing hardware, response-time requirements, geographic location, demand patterns and rack density. Infrastructure designed for large training clusters will not always be the most economical or appropriate option for every inference deployment. Data center operators and infrastructure leaders need to reassess how they design facilities and plan capacity to accommodate these different workload requirements. ## How inference workloads influence hardware selection Large-scale AI training relies on continuous computational throughput and high-speed communication among AI accelerators. However, inference has different infrastructure requirements because it must process incoming requests with low latency. Smaller models and some enterprise applications can run on CPUs. These processors support preprocessing, request handling and application orchestration. By contrast, larger generative models require GPUs for their parallel processing capabilities and high memory bandwidth. Factors such as model size, memory requirements and the number of simultaneous requests determine how much computing capacity an application requires. For example, a classification system that processes infrequent requests does not require the same infrastructure as a large language model ([LLM](https://www.techtarget.com/whatis/definition/large-language-model-LLM)). However, some high-volume inferences can still require substantial accelerator capacity. For infrastructure teams, the starting point is the application's expected traffic, response time targets and processing requirements. These factors help determine if conventional servers, accelerator-equipped systems or larger GPU clusters are the right choice. ## Preparing power and cooling for AI inference Rack power density is the electrical load concentrated in a cabinet. More operators are reporting peak rack densities of 30 kW or higher, according to Uptime Institute's 2026 [survey](https://intelligence.uptimeinstitute.com/resource/uptime-institute-global-data-center-survey-2026). Nvidia's [GB200 NVL72](https://docs.nvidia.com/dgx/dgxgb200-user-guide/hardware.html) rack consumes approximately 120 kW at full load, which shows why operators cannot use average facility rack densities to size every inference deployment. They need to analyze the electrical distribution at the rack, row and facility levels. Inference demand varies with application traffic and concurrent requests. Capacity planning should therefore account for peak loads, electrical headroom and potential [future expansion](https://www.techtarget.com/it-infrastructure/tip/Composable-architecture-Future-proofing-AI-expansion). Operators should avoid relying solely on average utilization as a metric. Credit: SambaNova Systems SambaNova Systems Co-Founder and CEO Rodrigo Liang is betting on fast AI inference chips for agentic AI, with Intel, SoftBank and JPMorganChase on board In early 2026, takeover talks between [SambaNova Systems](https://aimagazine.com/company/sambanova-systems) and Intel had hit a standstill. Six months later, SambaNova emerged with an US$11bn valuation, backed by Intel as a strategic partner and investor rather than an owner. This turnaround highlights where the AI chip market is heading. While training giant models made NVIDIA the world’s most me-valued chipmaker, running those models for millions of users presents a different challenge. Speed and cost per token now decide which company wins. Consequently, SambaNova has pivoted towards the inference market. Its new SN50 chip is pitched squarely at the agentic AI era. > SambaNova’s US$11bn valuation highlights the central role that fast inference now plays in the enterprise AI stack > > Rodrigo Liang, Co-Founder and CEO at SambaNova Systems ## What is SambaNova’s tech ecosystem? Founded in 2017 and based in San Jose, US, SambaNova designs its own processors, which it terms Reconfigurable Dataflow Units. Rather than selling chips in isolation, the company packages them into full systems and services. These services include SambaCloud for developers and SambaStack and SambaManaged for operators who want to run their own inference clouds. It also offers SambaRack hardware for on-premises deployment. The SN50, unveiled in February 2026, serves as the centrepiece of this technology ecosystem. SambaNova claims it runs up to five times faster than competing chips at up to three times lower total cost of ownership. The chip links up to 256 accelerators and supports models with more than 10 trillion parameters. These performance figures have helped the business win serious customers across multiple sectors. [Rodrigo Liang](https://aimagazine.com/executive/rodrigo-liang), Co-Founder and CEO at SambaNova Systems, says: “SambaNova’s US$11bn valuation highlights the central role that fast inference now plays in the enterprise AI stack.” Rodrigo Liang, Co-Founder and CEO at SambaNova Systems. Credit: Rodrigo Liang/LinkedIn ## Enterprise clients deploying SambaNova hardware JPMorganChase selected SambaNova as an inference infrastructure partner and is deploying SN40 and SN50 systems on premises. SoftBank Corp. will be the first company to deploy the SN50 in its next-generation data centres in Japan. In addition, TEPCO Systems will distribute the technology across Japan’s power sector. In Europe, OVHcloud and Infercom have built inference services on SambaNova hardware. The relationship with Intel has evolved into a strategic partnership rather than a corporate acquisition. A multi-year collaboration covers an Intel Xeon-based AI cloud and joint selling initiatives across global markets. It also includes a blueprint for heterogeneous inference that uses GPUs for prefill, SambaNova chips for decode and Xeon 6 processors for agentic tools. Intel Chief Executive Lip-Bu Tan also chairs SambaNova’s board. Om joins Infinity from Meta Superintelligence Labs, where he worked on software infrastructure for the company’s internal AI training and inference chips. Arledge brings expertise in CUDA programming and GPU optimization, having developed educational courses on large language models and compute kernels that have reached more than two million learners. The appointments support Infinity’s development of Ignition, an autonomous AI research agent designed to generate, test and optimize the low-level software required to run AI models efficiently on different chip architectures. “We’re hiring engineers to solve the greatest engineering challenges of our generation,” said **Jeremy Nixon**, Founder and CEO of Infinity. Nixon said the company’s objective is to automate the development of inference software, reducing the time required to prepare new AI chips for running advanced models. Before joining Meta, Om worked at Lightmatter, where he developed collective communications software for the company’s Passage platform. He also contributed to research on Lightmatter’s Envise technology published in Nature and previously worked as an Internet of Things systems design engineer at Intel. Om holds a master’s degree in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science from the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor. Arledge, a self-taught CUDA and kernel engineer, has developed courses focused on training large language models and optimizing GPU compute operations. At Infinity, he will contribute to the company’s automated AI infrastructure development efforts. Infinity’s Ignition platform is designed to address a challenge facing emerging AI chip manufacturers: developing the software infrastructure needed to support competitive inference performance. While established chip platforms benefit from extensive software ecosystems, newer hardware architectures often require substantial engineering work to optimize AI models for production deployment. Infinity aims to automate portions of that process through AI agents that write, test and refine compute kernels based on hardware performance feedback. In a previously published case study involving chip developer d-Matrix, Infinity reported achieving 92% of a chip’s theoretical peak performance within 10 hours of initial hardware access. The company also reported running three frontier AI models end-to-end within 10 days. Infinity maintains a design partnership with d-Matrix, whose Corsair chip supports inference workloads through the Infinity d-Matrix Cloud. The company has also announced a collaboration with HP Inc. to optimize NVIDIA’s Nemotron 3 Super model on the HP ZGX Fury platform, powered by the NVIDIA GB300 Grace Blackwell Ultra Desktop Superchip. The conversation spends most of its time on the second — how Modal sources GPUs from roughly 25 clouds, why the market has shifted from spot capacity to three-year prepaid reservations, and why that "rectangle" of supply does not match how most AI workloads actually behave. The title's framing (compute comes in rectangles) is fair but narrow: it is one thread inside a broader discussion of Modal's product history, the surprise rise of its sandbox business, and how the company is scaling from about 200 to a projected 700 people. Bernhardsson is unusually well placed to talk about this. He built Spotify's first music recommendation system starting around 2008–2009, spent five years as CTO of Better.com growing its tech team from a handful to several hundred, and released the open-source workflow orchestrator Luigi before founding Modal in 2021. The reader should come away with a concrete picture of the GPU supply chain as it stood in late 2026, a clear model of why Modal thinks multi-tenant aggregation beats both neoclouds and on-prem, and a set of specific numbers on Modal's growth, headcount, and revenue mix. ## GPU capacity has shifted from spot to multi-year prepaid deals Bernhardsson's account of how Modal buys compute is the most operationally detailed part of the episode, and it describes a market that changed shape over roughly the prior 18 months. Through the end of 2025, he says, most of Modal's capacity came from hyperscaler spot instances and one-year reservations, spread across many regions and aggregated into what the company treats as a single global pool. That model broke down as Modal grew and as the cloud market tightened. The current picture, by his account: | Dimension | Earlier model (through ~end of 2025) | Current model (as of late 2026) | | --- | --- | --- | | Primary source | Hyperscaler spot + on-demand (AWS, GCP, later Azure) | ~25 clouds, including neoclouds and smaller regional providers | | Contract length | Spot (preemptible) and one-year reservations | Three-plus-year deals, often with meaningful upfront payment | | Organizational cost | Minimal procurement function | ~4 full-time procurement staff; ~10-person engineering team managing bare-metal capacity worldwide | | Ownership | Rents all capacity | Still rents all capacity; ownership "on the table" but not pursued | He is explicit that Modal does not own hardware: "we rent all the capacity so far." The engineering team he describes exists to handle the physical reality of rented bare metal — "bad drives and GPUs falling off the bus," network issues, and vendor reliability. Modal sends prospective vendors a spec sheet (IOPS, CPU passmark scores, north-south bandwidth) and often runs an acceptance test on a single node before committing.
